# Love, Anger, Madness

**Love, Anger, Madness** (French: *Amour, Colère et Folie*) is a 1968 collection of three linked novellas by Haitian author Marie Vieux-Chauvet. The work consists of three distinct but thematically connected narratives titled "Love," "Anger," and "Madness," each depicting different aspects of life under political oppression in Haiti. Published by Éditions Gallimard in Paris with the support of French feminist Simone de Beauvoir, the book was quickly suppressed in Haiti due to its critical portrayal of the Duvalier regime and did not reach a wider international audience until decades later. The work is now recognized as a significant contribution to Haitian literature and postcolonial studies.

# Publication and Suppression

Marie Vieux-Chauvet began writing the three novellas in 1964 and initially sent them to Simone de Beauvoir as separate manuscripts around 1967. Beauvoir, impressed by the work, recommended their publication as a single collection to the French publisher Éditions Gallimard, which published *Amour, Colère et Folie* in 1968. The collection was met with scorn from Haitian critics and sparked outrage among government authorities under dictator François Duvalier. Fearing retribution from the regime, Vieux-Chauvet's family, particularly her husband Pierre Chauvet who was in France at the time, intervened to suppress the book's circulation in Haiti. Pierre Chauvet purchased copies in the country and destroyed them to protect the family from political retaliation.

After the initial suppression, the work remained largely unavailable for three decades. Following Vieux-Chauvet's death in 1973 from a brain tumor while in exile in New York, a pirated copy of the book eventually circulated among Haitian literary circles. The work was officially republished in France in 2005. In 2009, an English translation by Rose-Myriam Réjouis and Val Vinokur was published, making the work accessible to English-speaking audiences. This translation was subsequently released by Modern Library in 2010 with an introduction by Haitian-American author Edwidge Danticat.

# Recognition and Awards

In 1986, thirteen years after Vieux-Chauvet's death, *Love, Anger, Madness* was awarded the Deschamps Prize, a Haitian literary award. This recognition helped establish the work's legitimacy within Haitian letters and contributed to renewed interest in Vieux-Chauvet's literary legacy. The 2009 English translation brought the work to international scholarly attention, and it has since been studied extensively in postcolonial literature courses and Haitian studies programs.

# Content and Structure

*Love, Anger, Madness* is structured as a triptych of novellas that gradually increase in emotional intensity and psychological complexity. Each novella explores different dimensions of oppression under the Duvalier regime, though the historical setting is positioned during and after the American occupation of Haiti in the 1920s-1930s rather than the contemporary 1960s political moment.

### Love

The first novella, "Love," is narrated through diary entries by Claire Clamont, the eldest of three sisters from an upper-class mulatto family. Claire has never married and lives a repressed emotional life, sharing her home with her younger sisters Annette and Félicia, and Félicia's husband Jean Luze. Claire harbors secret desire for Jean Luze, who becomes sexually involved with Annette while Félicia is pregnant. The family lives under constant surveillance and psychological terror inflicted by the local police chief, Commandant Calédu, who employs home searches, disappearances, murder, rape, and torture against the population. The narrative explores how familial jealousy, resentment, and suppressed sexuality interact with external political oppression, creating a toxic emotional environment shaped by class anxiety and colorism.

### Anger

"Anger" (sometimes translated as "Wrath") shifts perspective to a middle-class family whose land is seized by paramilitary forces dressed in black uniforms who plant stakes marking the family's property as confiscated. The family members respond differently to this assault on their material security and dignity: the grandfather and disabled grandson express outrage, while the son and his wife respond with fearful passivity. The elder daughter Rose becomes the focus of state terror when one of the militia leaders compels her into a month-long sexual assault, which she experiences as a form of martyrdom. The novella is structured with the formal qualities of Greek tragedy, depicting how state-sanctioned violence fragments family bonds and produces cascading psychological damage. The narrative emphasizes class resentment as a motivator of the paramilitary violence, with the militia leader—referred to as "the Gorilla"—deriving pleasure from violating a young woman from the class that previously dominated him.

### Madness

"Madness" is the shortest and most surreal of the three novellas. Set in a besieged town, it follows René, a poor poet who barricades himself in a family shack with three other poets as "devils"—the local paramilitary forces—rampage through the village, killing hundreds and depositing bodies at the church door. The four men survive for eight days on rum and syrup while reciting verse, their minds deteriorating under the combined effects of hunger, fear, and alcohol intoxication. René's experience of the siege is rendered in increasingly hallucinatory prose interspersed with poetry, blurring the line between external reality and internal psychological collapse. The novella ends ambiguously when René attempts to escape and repel the devils, but the "invasion" is ultimately revealed to be alcohol-induced delusion, with the body he believed to be human actually being a dead dog. The work suggests that under conditions of extreme oppression, the boundary between interior madness and objective political reality becomes indistinguishable.

# Themes and Context

*Love, Anger, Madness* engages with several interconnected themes central to understanding late-twentieth-century Haiti. The work portrays how the Duvalier dictatorship, which governed Haiti from 1957 onward and intensified its authoritarian control through the 1960s, produced psychological and social fragmentation at every level of society. Vieux-Chauvet explores the complicity of the educated mulatto elite—her own social class—in perpetuating systems of oppression, depicting how class anxiety and colorism make the upper classes vulnerable to moral corruption and collaboration with tyranny.

The novellas also examine gender and sexual violence as state mechanisms of control. In both "Love" and "Anger," female characters experience or witness sexual exploitation as part of the regime's power apparatus. The work suggests that patriarchal violence and state violence are interconnected systems that operate on similar psychological principles.

Vodou, the religious and spiritual tradition of Haiti, appears throughout the work, particularly in "Madness" where the poets invoke the *loas* (spirits) during their siege. However, Vieux-Chauvet presents Vodou not as exoticized folklore but as an integral aspect of Haitian intellectual and spiritual life.

# Literary Style and Reception

Vieux-Chauvet's prose style in *Love, Anger, Madness* has been characterized by scholars as theatrical and psychologically penetrating. The first novella uses intimate first-person narration to render Claire's neurotic interior life; the second employs a choral structure reminiscent of Greek drama to depict collective family trauma; and the third shifts into expressionist and hallucinatory modes as it charts psychological dissolution.

The work was initially dismissed by Haitian literary critics as either too political or too psychologically disturbing. However, with renewed publication and translation, scholars have come to recognize *Love, Anger, Madness* as a masterwork of political fiction that captures the subjective experience of living under dictatorship with unprecedented psychological realism. Literary critic Edwidge Danticat has noted that the fictional siege in "Madness" parallels the historical experience of a group of Haitian writers called *Les Araignées du soir* (Evening Spiders), who continued to meet and produce work in semi-secrecy during Duvalier's repression, and that Vieux-Chauvet was the only woman among this literary collective.

## Adaptations

Beninese playwright José Pliya adapted the novellas into a series of theatrical pieces between 2007 and 2008. Productions of "Amour" (Love) and "Colère" (Anger) were staged at L'Archipel in Guadeloupe in 2008, with a production of "Folie" (Madness) following in 2009.

## Legacy and Significance

*Love, Anger, Madness* has exerted considerable influence on subsequent Haitian literature and diaspora writing. The work served as an inspiration for other Haitian writers, including Edwidge Danticat, whose own novels engage with similar themes of state violence, gender, and exile. Vieux-Chauvet's unflinching portrayal of complicity and psychological damage under dictatorship established a literary model for representing political trauma that extends beyond the Haitian context.

The work's trajectory—from suppression and exile to rediscovery and international recognition—also illustrates the precarious status of politically engaged literature under authoritarian regimes and the importance of preserving and translating works that challenge dominant narratives.

Love Anger, Madness by Marie Vieux-Chauvet tr. Rose Myriam-Réjouis, Val Vinokur
===============================================================================

### A Haitian Trilogy – Introduction by Edwidge Danticat

![Image 2: Love Anger Madness Marie Vieux Chauvet](https://clairemcalpine.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/love-anger-madness-marie-vieux-chauvet-1.jpg?w=660)Originally published in French as _Amour, colère et folie_, this trilogy of novellas was originally suppressed upon its initial publication in 1968. Seen as a scathing response to the struggles of race, class and sex that had occurred in Haiti, this major work became an underground classic, would send its author into exile and would finally be released in an authorised edition in France in 2005 (this English version in 2009).

Considered by [**Edwidge Danticat**](https://edwidgedanticat.com/about) as the cornerstone of Haitian literature, she opens her introduction telling us that “Fewer than a handful of Haitian writers have, both while alive and dead, inspired as much adulation, analysis, and discussion as **Marie Vieux-Chauvet**.”

Born in Port-au-Prince in 1916, **Marie Vieux-Chauvet** was a member of the “occupation generation”, that is, born a year after the United States invaded Haiti, an occupation that would last 19 years. She would use the turmoil of that rebellion as the back-story for _Love_, the first novella of the trilogy.

> “We have been practicing at cutting each other’s throats since Independence,” she writes of the country we Haitians like to remind the world was the first black republic in the Western Hemisphere, home to the only slave revolt that succeeded in producing a nation. What we would rather not say, and what Claire Clamont and Marie Vieux-Chauvet are brave enough to say, is that this same country has continued to fail at reaching its full potential, in part because of foreign interference and domination, but also because of internal strife and power struggles.

In three distinct novellas it unflinchingly manages to condemn totalitarianism and tyranny, with little care of the consequences, an act of courageousness or recklessness, but one that would make a significant and permanent mark in the chronicles of Haitian literature.

#### Love

The narrator of _Love_, Claire Clamont, is the eldest of three daughters, of a landowning upper-class family. She is the son her father never had and he wishes her to runs things as he would have them done. However, he hasn’t reckoned on her stubbornness and refusal to affiliate with some of the old ways he indulges, having raised her to think of them as superstitious. As a result she is neither feared nor respected by the workers, whom he had sold parcels of land to fund his political campaigns, a futile effort that has left the family near penniless.

The three sisters of this aristocratic family live together, all coveting the same man, Felicia’s husband. Annette succeeds in seducing him, Claire silently, voyeuristically encouraging her.

Meanwhile, a man sent to reform Haiti is known to use violent, torturous means to get his message across, preying on the innocent.

The love this elder daughter practices is tinged with jealousy, revenge and resentment, laying blame at the feet of an ancestor with dark skin. She resents this ancestor who made her so, resents her father for trying to turn her into the son he never had, resents one sister for marrying a man she loves and the other for having seduced him.

#### Anger

Anger centres around a family and the day a group of black uniformed paramilitary seize their land, putting stakes in the ground, the grandfather and the young disabled grandson are indignant, the son and his wife wary and afraid, their older daughter Rose is practical, the young adult son Paul going crazy, desires revenge.

Men arrive and plant stakes in the ground of land belonging to a family, they wear black uniforms and invoke fear. Each of the family inside react. Then the concrete arrives. They’re seizing the land and building a wall.

The family is observed, tries to address the injustice, is compromised.

> The mother got up slowly, put down her needlework, walked over to the old man and spoke into his ear.
> 
> “Look at him, Grandfather,” she whispered, “just look at him.”
> 
> The child was clenching his fists and grinding his teeth.
> 
> “Who will flog those who have taken our land?” he said without paying any attention to the mother. “Is there no longer a steward who can do it?”
> 
> “Alas, no!” the grandfather answered.
> 
> “Why not?”
> 
> “Because there are ups and downs in the life of a people. As the arrow rises, it gives birth to heroes; when it falls, only cowards come into the world. No steward would agree to stand up to those who have taken our land.”
> 
> He told himself that his crippled and sickly grandson was the faint beginning of the next era of heroes and that the arrow had begun its slow ascent only eight years ago. Hundreds more must have come into the world the same time he did, he thought, and with feet and legs as well as a brave soul. A day will come when they will grow up and the birds of prey will have to account for their deeds to every last one of them.

#### Madness

Madness is narrated by René, a lower class mulatto poet hiding inside his shack, paranoid about what’s going on outside his door and inside his mind, finding solace in a bottle, in rituals to do with voodoo beliefs that most of his life he has rejected and the poet friends he fearfully opens his door to, to offer them refuge. Unclear, what is real and what is the projection of a man’s fearful mind, we read on, aware that under oppression anything is possible.

A thought provoking read that invites the reader to understand more about the historical and present situation in Haiti.

**![Image 3: Marie Vieux Chauvet](https://clairemcalpine.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/marie-vieux-chauvet.jpeg?w=660)Marie Vieux-Chauvet** was a Haitian novelist, poet and playwright, the author of five novels including _Dance on the Volcano, Fonds des Negres, Fille d’Haiti_ and _Les Rapaces_.

Her works focus on class, color, race, gender, family structure and the upheaval of Haitian political, economic and social society during the United States occupation of Haiti and the dictatorship of François Duvalier. She died in New York in 1973.

#### Further Reading

[Permanent Exile: On Marie Vieux-Chauvet](https://www.thenation.com/article/archive/permanent-exile-marie-vieux-chauvet/)

Love, Anger, Madness – Marie Vieux-Chauvet (1968)
-------------------------------------------------

September 3, 2018 by [heavenali](https://heavenali.wordpress.com/author/heavenali/ "Posts by heavenali")

![Image 1: love anger madness](https://heavenali.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/love-anger-madness.jpg?w=412&h=634)

**_Translated from French by Rose-Myriam Réjouis and Val Vinokur_**

My final read for August’s Women in Translation month was a book of three novellas, **Love, Anger, Madness: a Haitian triptych**. Knowing nothing about Haiti – expect that voodoo comes from there, I was fascinated to learn more. I didn’t know what to expect from it really – and had never heard of the author at all.

> “Fear is a vice that takes root once it is cultivated. It takes time to recover from it.”

Marie Vieux-Chauvet was born in 1916 in the Haitian capital, part of what was called the ‘occupation generation’ – it was the year after the US invaded Haiti. She grew up in a tumultuous period in Haiti history, and this is very much reflected in these three novellas. In 1968 following the publication of this novel and the resulting furore Marie Vieux-Chauvet was exiled to the United States.

These stories depict families and artists struggling to survive, find love and safety in Haiti while living under some of the most terrifying and hostile conditions.

The first novella, **Love** is told in the form of a journal, by Claire, the eldest of three sisters, who has never married. Her younger two sisters, and her brother-in-law share the old family home with Claire – but there is jealousy and resentment at the heart of this family. As the novel opens, Félicia; the middle sister married to Jean Luze is in the early stages of pregnancy. The youngest sister Annette only twenty-two, is openly conducting an affair with her handsome brother-in-law. Claire is driven to distraction, not at the betrayal of her other sister, but because she too has developed a passion for Jean Luze. In time, Claire becomes devoted to her little nephew when he comes along, and as Félicia becomes more and more fragile and less present in the house, Claire begins to feel as if he is almost her own. With Jean Luze soon tired of Annette, this youngest sister, vain and self-serving, leaves, marrying someone else – and Claire’s fantasies about her brother-in-law increase.

> “Jean Luze plays a record in the living room. The notes penetrate me as he listens to them. My senses begin to vibrate so much that I rush to lock myself in my room. The sound explodes like a scream and then lingers in a caress. The entire house is suffused with it. What a hymn to life, this work born of suffering.”

This story of domestic disharmony takes place within a small, frightened community. The commandant, whose jail is across the street from Claire’s house, holds the community in thrall. We are witness to cruelty, fear and tales of sexual violence metered out to neighbours. Claire can hear the screams from her room.

In **Anger**, we meet the Normil family – with the story is told from multiple perspectives. One morning this large middle-class family wake to find militia men in black uniforms driving stakes into the ground around their home. This act of land seizure terrifies and intimidates the family, who have been proud landowners for many years. Rose, the pretty twenty-year old daughter becomes central to the crimes committed against this family and focus of much of the anger. For a month Rose must submit to the attentions of one of the militia leaders. Rose seeing herself as a martyr, goes to her fate in scenes which make for very uncomfortable reading. Meanwhile her mother, father, brothers and grandfather each deal differently with the unfolding situation. Their anger manifesting in various, destructive ways.

> “Louis Normil felt his father’s anger rising in him. The shock was what saved him. He instinctively tilted his head to take his leave of the lawyer and made for the exit. He thought he caught a glint of mockery in the guard’s eyes, but he paid him no mind and went to work.”

The third novella **Madness** is harder to talk about without completely ruining it. It is that shortest of the three novellas, and the one I liked the least. The story is narrated by a young poet; Rene. Trapped for days inside his house, he watches ‘the devils’ as he calls them through the shutters of the windows, as they rampage their way around the town. There is a body in the street outside and flies have started to gather on it. Opening the door to two friends, brothers and fellow poets Rene encourages them inside to hide from ‘the devils’ who are invading their town. Isolated and terrified – Rene is suffering from a lack of food and water, stealing himself for a last stand against authority.

Despite the fact not all of Vieux-Chauvet’s characters are likeable this triptych remains sympathetic. It is however, also brutal and uncompromising in its depiction of Haitian society, and the reality of a country in turmoil. It is brave and terrifyingly honest.

It really was no wonder that I needed a palate cleanser after this book – which runs to almost 400 pages – and began reading something entirely different a couple of hours after finishing it.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

| Marie Vieux-Chauvet
 |
| --- |
| [![Image 2: Vieux-Chauvet, Port-au-Prince 1963](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/a3/Marie_Vieux_Chauvet_by_Anthony_Phelps.jpg/250px-Marie_Vieux_Chauvet_by_Anthony_Phelps.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Marie_Vieux_Chauvet_by_Anthony_Phelps.jpg "Vieux-Chauvet, Port-au-Prince 1963")Vieux-Chauvet, Port-au-Prince 1963

 |
| Born | Marie Vieux

  
16 September 1916  

[Port-au-Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port-au-Prince "Port-au-Prince"), [Haiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Haiti_/(1859-1957/) "Republic of Haiti (1859-1957)")



 |
| Died | 19 June 1973 (aged 56)  

[New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State "New York State"), U.S.



 |
| Pen name | Colibri |
| Occupation | [Writer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writer "Writer") |
| Period | c. 1947–1973 |
| Genre | Novels, plays, short stories |

**Marie Vieux-Chauvet** (French pronunciation: [\[maʁi vjø ʃovɛ\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French"); born **Marie Vieux**; 16 September 1916 – 19 June 1973) was a Haitian novelist, playwright, and short story writer. Her novels are considered by translator [Myriam J. A. Chancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myriam_J._A._Chancy "Myriam J. A. Chancy") to be "by far the best-known works by a Haitian woman novelist". Born in [Port-au-Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port-au-Prince "Port-au-Prince"), Chauvet grew up during the [United States occupation of Haiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_occupation_of_Haiti "United States occupation of Haiti"). She began writing at the age of 10 and attended the Annex of the Upper School for Teachers, receiving her certificate in 1933. During the late 1940s, she wrote several plays, and during the 1950s, she wrote her first three novels. She became involved with the literary collective Haïti Littéraire during the early 1960s.

Chauvet sparked controversy in 1968 with the publication of _[Amour, Colere et Folie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness "Love, Anger, Madness")_ (transl. 'Love, Anger, Madness'), a collected trilogy of short novels. The book was met with disdain from Haitian critics and, for unclear reasons, suppressed and withdrawn from circulation. After the novel's suppression, facing threats from the regime of dictator [François Duvalier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Duvalier "François Duvalier"), Chauvet went into exile in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), where she died from a brain tumor. Her fifth book, _Les Rapaces_ (transl. 'Birds of Prey'), was published posthumously in 1986. Her work is noted by scholars such as Sophie Mariñez for its theatrical style, with common themes including gender, race, sexual violence, and [Haitian Vodou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haitian_Vodou "Haitian Vodou"). She has served as an inspiration for other Haitian writers such as [Edwidge Danticat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwidge_Danticat "Edwidge Danticat") and [Ghislaine Charlier](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ghislaine_Charlier&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ghislaine Charlier (page does not exist)") ([ht](https://ht.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghislaine_Charlier "ht:Ghislaine Charlier")).

Marie Vieux-Chauvet was born Marie Vieux in [Port-au-Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port-au-Prince "Port-au-Prince") on 16 September 1916. Her father, Constant Vieux, was a Haitian ambassador and senator, and her mother, Delia Nones, was of Jewish [West Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Indies "West Indies") descent.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover2016-1) Her early years were spent under the [United States occupation of Haiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_occupation_of_Haiti "United States occupation of Haiti"), during which the United States instituted various socioeconomic and political reforms, including seizing land to create foreign-owned [plantations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plantation "Plantation") and re-instituting [forced labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_labor "Forced labor"), violently repressing resistance.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmidt1995178Hallward200714Podur201213Glover2016-2) Her father, who was a member of the Haitian anti-occupation group Union Patriotique and editor of the anti-occupation periodical _Le Courier Haitien_, provided her with a political education.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover2016Jean-Louis202020,_142-3) She began writing at the age of 10, eventually attending the Annex of the Upper School for Teachers, an educational institute that trained [primary school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_school "Primary school") instructors.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012231Glover2016-4) She earned her certificate in 1933.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover2016-1) The occupation ended a year later, in 1934, with the withdrawal of American troops.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmidt1995xiii-5) At some point, she married physician Aymon Charlier. The couple had two daughters, Régine and Erma, before divorcing.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012231-6) She subsequently married travel agent Pierre Chauvet. The couple had one son, Pierre.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover2016-1)

During the 1940s, Chauvet wrote two plays. The first, _La Legende des fleurs_ (transl. 'The Flowers' Tale'), is an [allegory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegory "Allegory") where flowers in a garden stand in as a metaphor for gender dynamics within society.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJean-Charles201919Mari%C3%B1ez2020152-7) It was published under the pen-name "Colibri" (transl. 'Hummingbird') some time between 1947 and 1949.[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-Legendedate-9)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199360Jean-Charles201915Mari%C3%B1ez2020152-8) Her second play, _Samba_, was unpublished but first staged in 1948.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMari%C3%B1ez2020152-10)

In 1954, Chauvet wrote the short story "Ti-Moune nan bois" (transl. 'Little Moune in the woods'), which was published in _Optique_.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVitiello2021-11) She also published her first novel, _Fille d'Haiti_ (transl. 'Daughter of Haiti'), that same year. _Fille d'Haiti_, which won the 1954 Alliance Française Prize, tells the story of Lotus, the child of a [sex worker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_worker "Sex worker"), whose origins alienate her from her middle-class surroundings.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199358%E2%80%9359Vitiello2021-12) In 1957, she published her second novel, _La Danse sur le volcan_ (transl. 'Dance on the Volcano'), a [historical novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_fiction "Historical fiction") about a [mulatto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mulatto_Haitians "Mulatto Haitians") opera singer set during the [Haitian Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haitian_Revolution "Haitian Revolution").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199359Glover2016-13) Her third novel, _Fonds-des-nègres_ (transl. 'Negro Bottom'), was published in 1960, winning the France-Antilles Prize for that year.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199359Vitiello2021-14) It explores the role of [Vodou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haitian_Vodou "Haitian Vodou") in Haitian society through the eyes of Marie-Ange, a woman from Port-au-Prince who tries to help the impoverished inhabitants of a small village.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199359-15)

Throughout the 1960s, Chauvet became involved with Haïti Littéraire, a loose collective of politically-oriented artists and poets who sought to broaden Haitian literature beyond its nationalist focus, advocating for a more human-centered approach to writing and promoting cultural and educational initiatives through a variety of artistic mediums.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDash1981203%E2%80%93204Kruidenier_Tolliver2012231Glover2016-16) Chauvet's exact relationship to the group is disputed. According to researcher Julie-Françoise Tolliver, Chauvet "belonged" to Haïti Littéraire.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012231-6) However, according to researcher Kaiama L. Glover, she was only tangentially involved with the group during the early 1960s.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover2016-1) According to researcher Joëlle Vitiello, she hosted the group in her home on Sundays.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVitiello2021-11)

### _Amour, Colère et Folie_

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marie_Vieux-Chauvet&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Amour, Colère et Folie")\]

Chauvet began corresponding with French feminist [Simone de Beauvoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir "Simone de Beauvoir") in 1967, asking Beauvoir to recommend her writing to French publisher [Éditions Gallimard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89ditions_Gallimard "Éditions Gallimard").[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJoseph201530%E2%80%9331-17) She also described the oppressive conditions faced by writers under [François Duvalier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Duvalier "François Duvalier"), whose dictatorship began a decade earlier in 1957 and saw an escalation of state violence deployed by the [Tonton Macoute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonton_Macoute "Tonton Macoute"), a paramilitary and secret police force.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJoseph201532Kim2016-18) In 1968, Chauvet wrote _[Amour, Colere et Folie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness "Love, Anger, Madness")_ (transl. 'Love, Anger, Madness'), a collected trilogy of short novels.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199359Glover2016-13) _Amour_ depicts a woman named Claire through her diary entries, _Colère_ tells the story of a family whose land is confiscated by a military commander,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199359-15) and _Folie_ follows a group of mad poets trapped in a shack by an invasion of "devils", a term used to describe local paramilitary forces.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDash1998111%E2%80%93112Dize2022180-19) Chauvet submitted the trilogy to Beauvoir upon its completion, after which Beauvoir recommended it to Éditions Gallimard for publication.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover2016-1)

After its publication, _Amour, Colère et Folie_ was met with public scorn from Haitian critics and withdrawn from circulation.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012231%E2%80%93232-20) Various accounts are given of these events. Writer [Madison Smartt Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Smartt_Bell "Madison Smartt Bell") claims that Chauvet herself convinced Éditions Gallimard to withdraw the book from publication.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmartt_Bell2011-21) According to [Myriam J. A. Chancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myriam_J._A._Chancy "Myriam J. A. Chancy"), Pierre and his family suppressed its distribution by buying back unsold copies and forbidding translation, fearing government reprisal due to the trilogy's criticism of the Duvalier regime. Translator Rose-Myriam Réjouis claims the book's distribution was canceled due to concerns about the safety of Chauvet's family expressed by the Haitian ambassador to France. Academic Frank Laraque claims Editions Gallimard agreed to limit publicity for the book due to pressure from "spineless and cowardly people", hoping to protect the author's relatives who remained in Haiti.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012232%E2%80%93233-22)

Discouraged by the suppression of _Amour, Colère et Folie_ and facing threats from the regime, Chauvet left her husband and Haiti in 1969.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJoseph201535Glover2016-23) While she had initially considered [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") as a candidate for immigration, she ultimately opted to move to [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), moving from one apartment to another in [Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens "Queens") before settling in the [Upper East Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_East_Side "Upper East Side").[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJoseph201535-24) In 1970, she married Ted Proudfoot, an American petroleum industry worker.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover2016-1) In a letter dated 14 May 1971, she indicated that she was writing a book discussing her exile and relationship with Proudfoot.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012236-25) According to a subsequent letter dated 18 June 1971, she may have also moved to [Bronxville, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronxville,_New_York "Bronxville, New York").[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJoseph201535-24) At some point during her exile, she completed the manuscript for _Les Rapaces_ (transl. 'Birds of Prey'), a novella told from the perspective of a young girl and a cat.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBenedicty-Kokken201569Glover2016-26) However, she died on 19 June 1973 of a brain tumor before it could be released.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012230Joseph201530-27) It was published posthumously in 1986, over a decade after her death.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199359-15) She was working on two other books at the time of her death as well: _Les Fils d'Ogoun_ (transl. 'The Sons of Ogou') and _Le Cri_ (transl. 'The Cry').[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDayan1998119%E2%80%93120-28)

Writing and reception
---------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marie_Vieux-Chauvet&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Writing and reception")\]

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Marie_Vieux_Chauvet.jpg/250px-Marie_Vieux_Chauvet.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Marie_Vieux_Chauvet.jpg)

An illustration of Chauvet by artist Claire Gaudriot

Various sources discuss Chauvet's early dramatic work, particularly _La Légende des fleurs_. According to researcher Alessandra Benedicty-Kokken, the play analyzes societal notions of race, ultimately reflecting on the "tragically violent and humiliating consequences of Whiteness".[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBenedicty-Kokken2019222-29) Literary scholar Régine Michelle Jean-Charles gives an [ecofeminist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecofeminism "Ecofeminism") reading of the play, arguing that it uses its nature allegory to examine racial and gendered hierarchies. She describes the interconnected interactions of the flowers with each other and with the surrounding environment as representing an "ecological perspective", noting the uneven power dynamics between the flowers (which use feminine pronouns) and the sun, the butterfly, and the nightingale (which use masculine pronouns).[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJean-Charles201919%E2%80%9323-30) Researcher Sophie Mariñez posits that there is a "compelling case" that performance and theatricality, as exemplified in Chauvet's theatrical work, are defining elements of Chauvet's fiction as a whole.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMari%C3%B1ez2020152-10)

Glover identifies class, gender, race, and sexuality as common themes in Chauvet's first three novels.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover2016-1) She argues that _Fille d'Haïti_ is a reflection of the political upheaval taking place in Haiti in 1946 under [Élie Lescot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89lie_Lescot "Élie Lescot"), examining contemporary color-based tensions and foreshadowing François Duvalier's eventual rise to power.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover20137%E2%80%9321-31) Meanwhile, in discussing _La Danse sur le volcan_, researcher Curtis Small argues that Chauvet uses historical reconstruction to explore themes of gender and sexuality.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmall2009240;_242-32) Literary scholar Raphael Dalleo argues that the novel reflects Haitian [anticolonialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonization "Decolonization") while also depicting the race, class, and gender-based tensions of the revolutionary struggle.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDalleo2011129%E2%80%93130-33) Glover characterizes _Fonds-des-nègres_ as a critique of systemic corruption and gendered violence across Haitian society, while historian and literary critic Carrol F. Coates highlights its depiction of rural [Vodou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haitian_Vodou "Haitian Vodou") culture and the protagonist's transformative journey from alienation to spiritual belonging.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieux-ChauvetCoates1991564Glover2016-34) [Colin Dayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Dayan "Colin Dayan") similarly notes the use of Vodou in the novel, discussing how Chauvet's portrayal diverges from typical idealized and academic representations, instead grounding the religion in the material realities of the Haitian poor.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDayan199882%E2%80%9383-35)

In _Amour, Colère et Folie_, researchers [Lizabeth Paravisini-Gebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lizabeth_Paravisini-Gebert "Lizabeth Paravisini-Gebert") and Olga Torres-Seda identify themes of sexual and political repression.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199359-15) Tolliver highlights the book's portrayal of violence against women, as well as its variety of narrative styles and its depictions of oppression, martyrdom, and resistance.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012229,_240%E2%80%93241-36) Glover and researcher Keisha Simone Allan discuss the character Claire's feelings of inferiority in _Amour_, linking them to [Frantz Fanon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frantz_Fanon "Frantz Fanon")'s concept of "[epidermalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Skin,_White_Masks "Black Skin, White Masks")", a term Fanon uses to denote the practice of associating black skin with inferiority and the difficulties this association imposes on black people.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover201318Hein%C3%A4maaJardine2021315Allan202395-37) Jean-Charles discusses the deployment of sexual violence in the book, characterizing the rape of the character Rose in _Colère_ as being representative of social discourses surrounding [rape culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rape_culture "Rape culture").[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJean-Charles200616-38) Analyses of _Folie_ discuss its portrayal of the role of intellectuals under the Duvalier regime. Dash argues that it portrays the novel's protagonists as tragically flawed figures trapped by their self-centered ideals while Dalleo argues that it offers a more conflicted perspective, mourning the exhaustion of an anticolonial ideal while distinguishing the protagonists from middle-class collaborators with the authoritarian regime.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDash1998113%E2%80%93114Dalleo2011143%E2%80%93144-39)

_Les Rapaces_, Chauvet's posthumously-published novella, is described by Glover as a reflection on the regime of [Jean-Claude Duvalier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Claude_Duvalier "Jean-Claude Duvalier"), François's son.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover2016-1) Meanwhile, Benedicty-Kokken describes _Les Rapaces_ as a formally experimental work that critiques totalitarianism, contemporary [biopolitics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biopolitics "Biopolitics"), and the emergence of a [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights") paradigm dominated by [capitalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitalism "Capitalism"), the [bourgeoisie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourgeoisie "Bourgeoisie"), and the United States.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBenedicty-Kokken201557%E2%80%9358,_66%E2%80%9373-40)

According to Chancy, Chauvet's novels are "by far the best-known works by a Haitian woman novelist", inspiring other Haitian writers like [Ghislaine Charlier](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ghislaine_Charlier&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ghislaine Charlier (page does not exist)") ([ht](https://ht.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghislaine_Charlier "ht:Ghislaine Charlier")).[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChancy19978-41) Writer [Edwidge Danticat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwidge_Danticat "Edwidge Danticat") also cites her as an inspiration.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTETucker2019-42) In 1986, she was posthumously awarded the Deschamps Prize, which is awarded annually to works written in French or a [French-based creole language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French-based_creole_languages "French-based creole languages"), for _Amour, Colère, et Folie_.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVitiello2021Fondation_Lucienne_Deschamps-43) Excerpts from her work were published in the 1989 anthology _Her True-true Name_ and the 1992 anthology _[Daughters of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daughters_of_Africa "Daughters of Africa")_.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMordecaiWilson198984%E2%80%9389Busby1992271%E2%80%93275-44) Beninese playwright José Pliya adapted _Amour_, from _Amour, Colère, et Folie_, into a play in 2007. The play is an [abridged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abridgement "Abridgement") three-part monologue focusing on the character Claire.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller2019165%E2%80%93167-45) Adaptations of _Colère_ and _Folie_ were also produced and staged between 2007 and 2008 in [Guadeloupe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadeloupe "Guadeloupe").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVitiello2021-11) In 2016, on the [centennial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centennial "Centennial") of Chauvet's birth, celebratory activities were organized in cities across the world, including New York City, Port-au-Prince, and [Montreal, Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal,_Quebec "Montreal, Quebec").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVitiello2021-11) As part of the centennial, a symposium on Chauvet was held, during which artist and academic [Gina Athena Ulysse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Athena_Ulysse "Gina Athena Ulysse") read excerpts from Chauvet's work; theater director [Alice Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Reagan "Alice Reagan") dramatized readings from _La Legende des fleurs_, _Les Rapaces_, and an unpublished draft of _Amour_; and scholar Lena Taub Robles translated Pliya's adaptation of _Amour_ into English.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaub_Robles2019180-46)

[### Bad movie, excellent acting...](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0113729/reviews/?featured=rw0366789&ref_=tt_ururv_c_1_hd)

Like many other reviewers, I feel this is a poor movie (screenplay), but Drew really captures the feeling of mental illness. I've known some people who are manic depressive (and a few schizophrenics) and I have to say that Drew must have some personal knowledge of severe depression to be able to pull off a performance like this. She really elevates the movie from a 2-bit teen romance and makes it worth watching. I'm not generally a fan (\*hated\* Donnie Darko) and I usually find her childish "damaged goods" image rather irritating even though it may be her real personality, but in this one she just embodies the part. 6/10.

[### Mad Overdrive](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0113729/reviews/?featured=rw3221837&ref_=tt_ururv_c_3_hd)

Shirtless in Seattle, handsome blue-eyed Chris O'Donnell (as Matt Leland) has his telescope trained on jiggling blonde Drew Barrymore (as Casey Roberts). Later, the sexy high school seniors go to a concert by themselves, which is strange, and do some head-banging. They skip school and have fun driving her yellow Volkswagen around town. These two are attractive, affluent and in love. However, something seems wrong. To be with Mr. O'Donnell during a test, Ms. Barrymore pulls the school fire alarm. "What are you, nuts?" asks O'Donnell. "Yeah," she replies. This turns out to be true...  
  
Director Antonia Bird gets all her spark plugs in line for a fine sequence involving traveling salesman Liev Schreiber...  
  
Barrymore seems emotionally disturbed, with a confidential diagnosis. After a suicide attempt, she is committed. O'Donnell helps her bust out of the mental hospital and they go on a joyride to Mexico. Barrymore's road "games" are so obviously over the top, it's a stretch to believe O'Donnell doesn't catch on faster. Possibly, it would have worked better if writer Paula Milne gave him some substance abuse; the character seems too level-headed. Barrymore and O'Donnell look great together, but are unconvincing as an amateur "Bonnie and Clyde". Besides, it looks like car theft is legal in the southwest.  
  
\*\*\*\*\* Mad Love (5/26/95) Antonia Bird ~ Chris O'Donnell, Drew Barrymore, Kevin Dunn, Liev Schreiber

[### The Girl from Chicago](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0113729/reviews/?featured=rw3467362&ref_=tt_ururv_c_4_hd)

The high-school student Matt Leland (Chris O'Donnell) lives with his twin brother and sister and his father in a house by the lake. When the teenager Casey Roberts (Drew Barrymore) moves to the house on the other side of the lake, Matt snoops into her room with his telescope. They meet each other and soon they fall in love with each other. One day, Matt is taking a test at school and Casey activates the fire alarm to stop the test. She is suspended and her father decides to check her into a psychiatric institution. However Matt breaks her out of the hospital. They travel in Matt's car and have lots of fun until the day Matt discovers that Casey has bipolar disorder with periods of depression and periods of elevated mood. When she tries to commit suicide, Matt realizes that she needs specialized help.  
  
"Mad Love" is a road movie with a tale of madness and sort of teen version of "The Girl from Trieste". Matt Leland is a good student and son that changes his behavior when he falls in love with the maniac depressive Casey that has arrived from Chicago. When she is interned in an institution, he believes that her family is unfair with the girl. But when he realizes that her mental illness is serious and dangerous, he contacts her family and they find the solution for her treatment. My vote is seven.  
  
Title (Brazil): "Amor Louco" ("Mad Love")

[### ...by any other name](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0113729/reviews/?featured=rw0366790&ref_=tt_ururv_c_5_hd)

It seems like the title of this movie was chosen at the last minute by the guy in the business suit. "So it's about a coupla teenagers, let's say they're 'in love', and one of them has mental problems, let's call her crazy..." The film itself though, I think, resists cliches, especially the fact that the four letter word (love) was avoided, which has a tendency to suck dry any useful plot content that might be found in a movie, opting for some different ways of illustrating their relationship. The two main characters are well portrayed, and believable. I think Barrymore and O'Donnell hold together something that may not have great elements like soundtrack, plot originality etc, because despite the fact that Drew's eyebrows really annoyed me, they both did a good job.

Click here for more information.") From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Love, Anger, Madness

Cover of the 2009 English translation

AuthorMarie Vieux-Chauvet
Original titleAmour, Colère et Folie
TranslatorRose-Myriam Réjouis, Val Vinokur
LanguageFrench
PublisherÉditions Gallimard (withdrawn)
Maisonneuve et Larose (fr)/Emina Soleil
Modern Library

Publication date

1968 (original)
2005 (reprint)

Published in English

2009
AwardsDeschamps Prize (1986)
ISBN978-2-7068-1871-4 (French edition, 2005)
978-0-679-64351-7 (English edition, 2009)
_**Love, Anger, Madness**_ ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _Amour, Colère et Folie_) is a 1968 collection of short novels published by the Haitian author [Marie Vieux-Chauvet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet "Marie Vieux-Chauvet"). There are three novels in the collection: _Love_, _Anger_, and _Madness_. _Love_ depicts a woman named Claire through her diary entries, _Anger_ tells the story of a family whose land is confiscated by a group of men in black uniforms, and _Madness_ follows a group of mad poets trapped in a shack by an invasion of "devils", a term they use to describe the local paramilitary forces. Chauvet initially sent _Love_, _Anger_, and _Madness_ to French feminist [Simone de Beauvoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir "Simone de Beauvoir") as three individual manuscripts. Beauvoir recommended their publication as a single volume to the publisher [Éditions Gallimard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89ditions_Gallimard "Éditions Gallimard"), who published the collection in 1968. It was met with scorn from Haitian critics and, for unclear reasons, suppressed and withdrawn from circulation soon after its publication. After Chauvet's death in 1973, _Love, Anger, Madness_ was awarded the Deschamps Prize in 1986 and saw several new editions and translations, including an official French reprint in 2005[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-Frenched-2) and an English translation in 2009. Beninese playwright José Pliya adapted the book into a series of plays between 2007 and 2008. _Love_ (French: _Amour_) is told from the perspective of Claire Clamont, a [mulatto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mulatto_Haitians "Mulatto Haitians") woman who lives with her sisters Annette and Félicia, as well as Félicia's husband, Jean Luze. Through her diary entries, Claire narrates her repressed desire for Jean Luze, who is himself developing an interest in Annette. Meanwhile, the local police chief, Commandant Calédu, terrorizes the local populace through home searches, [disappearances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enforced_disappearance "Enforced disappearance"), murder, rape, and torture. One evening, Claire watches through a keyhole in the door as Jean Luze and Annette are involved in what appears to be a sexual encounter. Later, Félicia, who is pregnant, faints upon seeing Annette and Jean Luze together, forcing Jean Luze to end the affair. After Félicia gives birth to a boy named Jean-Claude, a heartbroken Annette attempts suicide but survives and marries the scion of an influential [Afro-Haitian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Haitian "Afro-Haitian") family. The story then shifts to an extended flashback, with Claire describing her upbringing, the [colorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorism "Colorism") she faced as a child as the darkest-skinned sister, and the loss of her family's land. Back in the present, Félicia becomes pregnant again, and Claire is tasked with taking care of Jean-Claude. As Félicia's pregnancy progresses, she falls ill, and Jean Luze takes her to [Port-au-Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port-au-Prince "Port-au-Prince") alongside Claire and Jean-Claude to receive an abortion. Upon returning from Port-au-Prince, Claire, tired of repressing her desires, plots to kill Félicia with a dagger so that she can be with Jean Luze. However, as a riot breaks out targeting Calédu and his American allies, she instead stabs Calédu in the back. _Anger_ (French: _Colère_) tells the story of the Normil family, whose land is seized by a group of men in black uniforms. The grandfather of the family is strongly opposed to relinquishing the land. The father vows to hold on to it, but his attempt to solicit assistance from a lawyer goes poorly. Rose, his daughter, is sexually harassed by one of the Blackshirts, who is visiting the lawyer's office, and the lawyer charges the family $500 upfront for his services. The father gets the money from his wealthy mistress, but the lawyer will not take it from him, insisting that Rose deliver it. Later, Rose's younger brother Paul sees her get into a car with the man from the lawyer's office, who is referred to as "the Gorilla". Realizing that Rose is having sex with the Gorilla, Paul vows to kill him. The story then switches perspectives from [third-person](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narration#third-person "Narration") to a series of [first person](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-person_narrative "First-person narrative") [stream of consciousness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stream_of_consciousness "Stream of consciousness") narrations. A section narrated by Rose describes her sadistic [rape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rape "Rape")[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-3) at the hand of the Gorilla. It is revealed that he told Rose that if she had sex with him regularly for a month, the family's plot would be restored. Meanwhile, the father sows division amongst the Blackshirts by selling the family's land in parcels, prompting the Blackshirts to argue over who gets what. In the ensuing conflict, one of the Gorilla's lieutenants shoots him. The grandfather is then killed by the Blackshirts alongside Rose and Paul's disabled brother. Rose dies from exhaustion soon afterward. _Madness_ (French: _Folie_) is a stream of consciousness narrative told from the perspective of René, a poet hiding in a shack while a group of uniformed paramilitaries referred to as "devils" besiege the town around him. He is soon joined by another poet, André. After Jacques, another poet, joins them, René plots a rebellion against the devils using homemade [Molotov cocktails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molotov_cocktail "Molotov cocktail"). Their numbers grow again with the arrival of a fourth poet, a white man named Simon. Jacques, who is naturally timid, passes out from fright when Simon suggests opening the doors and eventually dies. After this, René, in a fit of madness, runs into the street and throws a Molotov cocktail. After this, in an extended dramatic dialogue structured like a play, it is revealed that the poets have hallucinated the presence of the devils. The local police commandant arrests them for arson. Cécile, a woman living across the street, is accused of collaborating with them and arrested as well. The commandant interrogates the poets and orders their execution. René prays for aid from God, and the narrative ends with a vision of angels descending. Publication history ------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Love,_Anger,_Madness&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Publication history")\] [![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Marie_Vieux_Chauvet.jpg/250px-Marie_Vieux_Chauvet.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Marie_Vieux_Chauvet.jpg) An illustration of [Marie Vieux Chauvet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux_Chauvet "Marie Vieux Chauvet") by artist Claire Gaudriot Haitian author [Marie Vieux-Chauvet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet "Marie Vieux-Chauvet") began corresponding with French feminist [Simone de Beauvoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir "Simone de Beauvoir") in 1967, asking Beauvoir to recommend her writing to French publisher [Éditions Gallimard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89ditions_Gallimard "Éditions Gallimard").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJoseph201530%E2%80%9331-4) She also described the oppressive conditions faced by writers under [François Duvalier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Duvalier "François Duvalier"), whose dictatorship, beginning in 1957, saw an escalation of state violence deployed by the [Tonton Macoute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonton_Macoute "Tonton Macoute"), a paramilitary and secret police force.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJoseph201532Kim2016-5) In 1968, Chauvet wrote _Love, Anger, Madness_, her fourth book after _Fille d'Haiti_ (transl. 'Daughter of Haiti'), _La Danse sur le volcan_ (transl. 'Dance on the Volcano'), and _Fonds-des-nègres_ (transl. 'Negro Bottom').[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199358%E2%80%9359-6) She submitted the trilogy as three separate manuscripts to Beauvoir upon its completion, and Beauvoir recommended it to Éditions Gallimard for publication as a single volume.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012231-7) ### Initial release and controversy \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Love,_Anger,_Madness&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Initial release and controversy")\] After its publication in 1968, _Love, Anger, Madness_ was met with public scorn from Haitian critics.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012231-7) According to literary critic J. Michael Dash, the book's political boldness and its critique of the Haitian elite prevented it from achieving widespread acclaim.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDash1998110-8) For unclear reasons, it was also withdrawn from circulation.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012231%E2%80%93235-9) Various accounts are given of these events. Writer [Madison Smartt Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Smartt_Bell "Madison Smartt Bell") claims that Chauvet herself convinced Éditions Gallimard to withdraw the book from publication.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmartt_Bell2011-10) According to [Myriam J. A. Chancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myriam_J._A._Chancy "Myriam J. A. Chancy"), Pierre and his family suppressed its distribution by buying back unsold copies and forbidding translation, fearing government reprisal due to the trilogy's criticism of the Duvalier regime. Translator Rose-Myriam Réjouis claims the book's distribution was canceled due to concerns about the safety of Chauvet's family expressed by the Haitian ambassador to France. Academic Frank Laraque claims Editions Gallimard agreed to limit publicity for the book due to pressure from "spineless and cowardly people", hoping to protect the author's relatives who remained in Haiti.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012232%E2%80%93233-11) Discouraged by the suppression of _Amour, Colère et Folie_ and facing threats from the regime, Chauvet left her husband and Haiti in 1969 to move to [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJoseph201535Glover2016-12) She died of a brain tumor there on 19 June 1973.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012230Joseph201530-13) In 1986, she was posthumously awarded the Deschamps Prize, which is awarded annually to works written in French or a [French-based creole language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French-based_creole_languages "French-based creole languages"), for _Love, Anger, Madness_.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVitiello2021Fondation_Lucienne_Deschamps-14) ### Posthumous editions and translations \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Love,_Anger,_Madness&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Posthumous editions and translations")\] Several editions of _Love, Anger, Madness_ were published after Chauvet's death. An unauthorized edition based on scans of the 1968 edition was released by Voix de Femmes in 2003.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012238-15) Others were issued by [Maisonneuve et Larose](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Maisonneuve_et_Larose&action=edit&redlink=1 "Maisonneuve et Larose (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maisonneuve_et_Larose "fr:Maisonneuve et Larose")) in collaboration with Emina Soleil in 2005,[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-Frenched-2) by Zellige in 2008, and by [Zulma](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Zulma_\(publisher\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Zulma (publisher) (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zulma "fr:Zulma")) in 2015.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTESpear201513;_19-20Vitiello2021-16) German and Italian translations were released by [Ullstein Verlag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ullstein_Verlag "Ullstein Verlag") and [Bompiani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bompiani "Bompiani") respectively. A Serbian translation was released by [Laguna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_/(publisher/) "Laguna (publisher)") in 2008.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTESpear201520-17) In 2009, [Random House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_House "Random House") released an English translation by Rose-Myriam Rejouis and Val Vinokur under its [Modern Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Library "Modern Library") imprint.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTESpear201520Vitiello2021-18) Several scholars have analyzed Claire's feelings of inferiority in _Love_. Researchers Kaiama L. Glover and Keisha Simone Allan both tie these feelings to philosopher [Frantz Fanon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frantz_Fanon "Frantz Fanon")'s concept of "[epidermalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Skin,_White_Masks "Black Skin, White Masks")", a term Fanon uses to denote the practice of associating black skin with inferiority and the difficulties this association imposes on black people.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover201318Hein%C3%A4maaJardine2021315Allan202395-19) According to Glover, Claire's sexual repression is the result of her mother's "ill-disguised shame at having a brown-skinned daughter" and therefore the "bigotry of the bourgeois mulatto community".[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover201319-20) Allan also argues that Claire's feelings of self-loathing are "linked to the racial tensions in her socio-political milieu".[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllan202395-21) Both Glover and Allan tie Claire's personal struggle to the broader power inversion experienced by the mulatto community amidst the ascendancy of Caledu, who represents the [noirist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noirism "Noirism")[\[c\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-23) state.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover201319Allan202399-24) Allan also links her struggle to efforts by middle-class Haitians to distance themselves from their African ancestry.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllan202397-25) Scholars have also discussed the ways in which portrayals of race and class intersect with gender in _Love_. Researcher Hellen Lee-Keller argues that Claire's narrative critiques the economic, political, and social structures that limit women's political and public engagement.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee-Keller20091293-26) She singles out the ways that the demands imposed on Claire due to her class and gender conflict with those placed on her by her family, leading to the "fragmentation of \[her\] identity.".[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee-Keller20091297-27) Glover argues that Claire has internalized the hegemonic valuation of elite mulatto women's bodies as objects to be used in marital transactions, which contributes to her belief in her inferiority.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover201318%E2%80%9319-28) Researcher Kerstin Oloff Claire figuratively situates Claire within the [gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_fiction "Gothic fiction") tradition of the "female [zombie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zombie "Zombie")" whose soul and agency have been stolen, rendering her a compliant, atomized figure trapped by the patriarchal and capitalist structures of her society.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOloff2018128%E2%80%93129-29) _Love'_s portrayal of peasants has also been the subject of scholarly analysis. Lee-Keller discusses the peasants that work Claire's father's land, highlighting the contrast between their impoverished existence and the Clamont family's obscene wealth, which is built upon their labor and the family's ignorance of their suffering in a reflection of [slavery in Saint-Domingue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_Haiti "Slavery in Haiti").[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee-Keller20091308-30) Oloff argues that Chauvet uses gothic conventions to link Claire's figurative "zombification" to the exploitation of the Haitian peasantry and the environment, with the zombie figure acting as a displaced representation of the socio-ecological alienation and material exploitation caused by United States imperialism in the global imagination.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOloff2018125%E2%80%93126,_130%E2%80%93132-31) Literary scholar [Colin Dayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Dayan "Colin Dayan") observes that while Chauvet's peasants perform deference to Haitian elites, their apparent passivity is a survival strategy that masks subversive agency.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDayan199895%E2%80%9396-32) The classification of sexual violence in _Anger_ has been the subject of scholarly debate. Researcher Liddy Detar argues that Rose's sexual encounters with the Gorilla are best understood not as rapes, but as a form of political sexual torture, which systematically destroys the victim's language and world.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDetar2002203%E2%80%93204-33) She further argues that Rose "develops an intimacy with the Gorille on whom her own life depends" to reclaim her agency and confront her complicity in the exchanges, subverting the victim/torturer binary and acknowledging mulattos' role in the historical exploitation of Afro-Haitians.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDetar2002210%E2%80%93211-34) Dayan compares the encounters between Rose and the Gorilla to the myth of Sister Rose, a mythical Haitian woman whose rape is said to have founded the nation.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDayan199848,_122-35) She argues that Rose subverts this myth by "willingly offer\[ing\] herself in exchange for land".[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDayan1998122-36) Researcher [Elizabeth Walcott-Hackshaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Walcott-Hackshaw "Elizabeth Walcott-Hackshaw") characterizes this exchange as a "Faustian pact".[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWalcott-Hackshaw200545-37) Chancy describes the encounters as rapes, emphasizing their brutality while simultaneously stating that they come as a result of a "poor choice" by Rose, who attempts to protect her class status rather than "undo\[ing\] the harms of the dictatorship".[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChancy2004311-38) Researcher Régine Michelle Jean-Charles argues that what happens to Rose is rape because Rose submits her body "out of fear", which "obliterates the option of consent". Per Jean-Charles, Rose's rape is representative of the terror of the Duvalier regime, during which people's private lives "no longer belonged to them", and "is an example of how seizure by the state also extends to the female body".[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJean-Charles20067%E2%80%938-39) Researcher Laura Roldán-Sevillano concurs with Jean-Charles's assessment, describing the encounters as rapes and Rose as the Gorilla's "sex slave". She argues that while her family's fear and shame prevent them from helping her, she is empowered as a survivor through her own narrative voice presented at the end of the novel, challenging the culture of silence surrounding rape in Haiti.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTERold%C3%A1n-Sevillano202335%E2%80%9337-40) Analyses of _Madness_ discuss its portrayal of the role of intellectuals under the Duvalier regime. Dash argues that the novel's portrayal of René, whose fantasies of liberation are ultimately self-serving and authoritarian, reveals the Haitian intellectual under Duvalier to be a tragically flawed figure who is alienated from society and who mirrors the oppressive culture they seek to resist.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDash1998113%E2%80%93114-41) Literary scholar Raphael Dalleo argues that Dash's reading is reductive, countering that the novel takes a more "conflicted perspective" on Haitian intellectuals, mourning the exhaustion of a particular anticolonial modernist ideal while portraying the poets as victims of state terror—distinct from elements of the middle class collaborating with the authoritarian state.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDalleo2011143%E2%80%93144-42) Several scholars note _Madness'_s use of the [carnivalesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnivalesque "Carnivalesque") mode, first conceptualized by Russian literary scholar [Mikhail Bakhtin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Bakhtin "Mikhail Bakhtin") as a mode that uses popular humor to resist official hierarchies.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBirchHooper2012-43) Dash compares the structure of the novel to the structure of a carnival, describing the presence of the "devils" as a "gruesome masequerade". He concludes that the use of the carnivalesque mode in _Madness_ is a pessimistic illusion that reflects the "ludicrous nightmare" of Haitian society.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDash1998116%E2%80%93117-44) Researcher Charlee M. Redman Bezilla argues that _Madness_ contains elements of the Romantic [grotesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grotesque "Grotesque") and carnivalesque modes, creating a chaotic public spectacle that lacks the "regenerative aspect" of the carnivalesque but that still opens a space for revolt and social critique.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTERedman_Bezilla201982-45) The novel's use of religious themes is also noted by several scholars. Dayan highlights Chauvet's framing of [Haitian Vodou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haitian_Vodou "Haitian Vodou"), not as a system of abstract beliefs, but as a form of inheritance that resists modernity's attempts to erase it.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDayan199884-46) Meanwhile, Dash describes René's "esoteric spirituality" as a form of escape from the "psychic agony" he endures, comparing the poets to a "tiny, extremist sect". He also compares the poets' deployment of "images of martyrdom and apocalyptic rebirth" and their dreams of a "wrathful God, who with fire and brimstone will create order from the prevailing chaos" to the language used in the biblical [Book of Revelation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Revelation "Book of Revelation").[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDash1998115-47) Beninese playwright José Pliya adapted _Love_, from _Love, Anger, Madness_, into a play in 2007. The play is an [abridged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abridgement "Abridgement") three-part monologue focusing on the character Claire.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller2019165%E2%80%93167-48) Adaptations of _Anger_ and _Madness_ were also produced and staged between 2007 and 2008 in [Guadeloupe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadeloupe "Guadeloupe").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVitiello2021-1) 1. ^ [_**a**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_ref-Frenched_2-0) [_**b**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_ref-Frenched_2-1) According to Vitiello, this edition was released in 2004.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVitiello2021-1) 2. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_ref-3)** For brevity, this summary uses the word "rape" to describe what happens to Rose.
