| Signature |
| [![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Simone_de_Beauvoir_signature.svg/250px-Simone_de_Beauvoir_signature.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Simone_de_Beauvoir_signature.svg) |

**Simone Lucie Ernestine Marie Bertrand de Beauvoir** (, ;[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-4) French: [\[simɔn də bovwaʁ\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French") [](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/4/49/Fr-Simone_de_Beauvoir.ogg/Fr-Simone_de_Beauvoir.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fr-Simone_de_Beauvoir.ogg "File:Fr-Simone de Beauvoir.ogg"); 9 January 1908 – 14 April 1986) was a French [existentialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existentialism "Existentialism") philosopher, writer, [social theorist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_theorist "Social theorist"), and [feminist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feminism "Feminism") activist. Though she did not consider herself a philosopher, nor was she considered one at the time of her death,[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-7) she had a significant influence on both [feminist existentialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feminist_existentialism "Feminist existentialism") and [feminist theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feminist_theory "Feminist theory").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-SEP-Bergoffen-2010-8)

Beauvoir wrote novels, essays, short stories, biographies, autobiographies, and monographs on philosophy, politics, and social issues. She was best known for her "trailblazing work in feminist philosophy",[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-:0-9) _[The Second Sex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Second_Sex "The Second Sex")_ (1949), a detailed analysis of women's oppression and a foundational tract of contemporary [feminism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feminism "Feminism"). She was also known for her novels, the most famous of which were _[She Came to Stay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/She_Came_to_Stay "She Came to Stay")_ (1943) and _[The Mandarins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mandarins "The Mandarins")_ (1954).

Her most enduring contribution to literature are her memoirs, notably the first volume, _Mémoires d'une jeune fille rangée_[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-10) (1958).[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-11) She received the 1954 [Prix Goncourt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prix_Goncourt "Prix Goncourt"), the 1975 [Jerusalem Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerusalem_Prize "Jerusalem Prize"), and the 1978 [Austrian State Prize for European Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_State_Prize_for_European_Literature "Austrian State Prize for European Literature"). She was also nominated for the [Nobel Prize in Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "Nobel Prize in Literature") in [1961](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1961_Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "1961 Nobel Prize in Literature"), [1969](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "1969 Nobel Prize in Literature") and [1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "1973 Nobel Prize in Literature").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-12) However, Beauvoir generated controversy when she briefly lost her teaching job after being accused of sexually abusing some of her students.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-13)

Beauvoir was born on 9 January 1908,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-14) into a [bourgeois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourgeois "Bourgeois") [Parisian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") family in the [6th arrondissement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6th_arrondissement_of_Paris "6th arrondissement of Paris").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-15)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-16)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-17) Her parents were Georges Bertrand de Beauvoir, a lawyer who once aspired to be an actor,[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-IEP_Biography-18) and Françoise Beauvoir (née Brasseur), a wealthy banker's daughter and devout [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic "Catholic"). Simone had a sister, [Hélène](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9l%C3%A8ne_de_Beauvoir "Hélène de Beauvoir"), who was born two years later, on 6 June 1910. Beauvoir was intellectually precocious, fueled by her father's encouragement; he reportedly would boast,

> “Simone has a man's brain; she thinks like a man; she is a man.”[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-19)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-20)

— Françoise Beauvoir (née Brasseur), in Caroline Moorehead, A talk with Simone de Beauvoir, [The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")

Writing of her youth in _Memoirs of a Dutiful Daughter,_ she said:

> ...my father's [individualism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Individualism "Individualism") and pagan ethical standards were in complete contrast to the rigidly moral [conventionalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conventionalism "Conventionalism") of my mother's teaching. This disequilibrium, which made my life a kind of endless disputation, is the main reason why I became an [intellectual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual "Intellectual").[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-21)

— Simone de Beauvoir, Memoirs of a Dutiful Daughter, Book One

Beauvoir pursued post-secondary education after completing her high school years at [Cours Desir](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cours_Desir&action=edit&redlink=1 "Cours Desir (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cours_Desir "fr:Cours Desir")).[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-22) After passing baccalaureate exams in mathematics and philosophy at the age of seventeen in 1925, she studied mathematics at the [Institut Catholique de Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut_Catholique_de_Paris "Institut Catholique de Paris") and literature/languages at the [Institut Sainte-Marie](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Institut_Sainte-Marie&action=edit&redlink=1 "Institut Sainte-Marie (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut_Sainte-Marie "fr:Institut Sainte-Marie")).

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/EcoleNormaleDeParis_-_Jeanne_Blancard-Colette_Maze.tif/lossy-page1-250px-EcoleNormaleDeParis_-_Jeanne_Blancard-Colette_Maze.tif.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:EcoleNormaleDeParis_-_Jeanne_Blancard-Colette_Maze.tif)

Classe de l’[École Normale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_Normale "École Normale") de Paris, vers les années 1930. Envoi par l’Auteur - Fabrice Maze.

Although not officially enrolled, she sat in on courses at the [École Normale Supérieure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_Normale_Sup%C3%A9rieure "École Normale Supérieure") in preparation for the _[agrégation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agr%C3%A9gation "Agrégation")_ in philosophy, a highly competitive postgraduate examination that serves as a national ranking of students. It was while studying for it that she met École Normale students [Jean-Paul Sartre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Paul_Sartre "Jean-Paul Sartre"), [Paul Nizan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Nizan "Paul Nizan"), and [René Maheu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Maheu "René Maheu") (who gave her the lasting nickname "_Castor_", or "Beaver").[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-IEP_Biography-18) She studied philosophy at the [Sorbonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Paris "University of Paris") and after completing her degree in 1928, wrote her _[Diplôme d'études supérieures spécialisées](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dipl%C3%B4me_d%27%C3%A9tudes_sup%C3%A9rieures_sp%C3%A9cialis%C3%A9es "Diplôme d'études supérieures spécialisées")_ (roughly equivalent to an [M.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Arts "Master of Arts") thesis) on [Leibniz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gottfried_Wilhelm_Leibniz "Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz") for [Léon Brunschvicg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9on_Brunschvicg "Léon Brunschvicg") in 1929 (the topic was "Le concept chez Leibniz" \["The Concept in Leibniz"\]).[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-23) In 1929 the jury for the _agrégation_ narrowly awarded Sartre first place and gave second to Beauvoir. She was 21 years old which made her the youngest person to ever pass the exam.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-24) Additionally, Beauvoir finished an exam for the certificate of "General Philosophy and Logic" second to [Simone Weil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_Weil "Simone Weil"). Her success as the eighth woman to pass the _agrégation_ solidified her economic independence.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-:0-9)

#### Religious upbringing

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Simone_de_Beauvoir&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Religious upbringing")\]

Beauvoir was raised Catholic and educated in convent schools. She was deeply religious and intended to become a nun. At age 14 Beauvoir began to question her faith and would go on to abandon religion in her teens. She remained an [atheist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atheism "Atheism") for the rest of her life.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-auto-25)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Thurman-26) To explain her atheist beliefs, Beauvoir stated,

> "Faith allows an evasion of those difficulties which the atheist confronts honestly. And to crown all, the believer derives a sense of great superiority from this very cowardice itself."[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-27)

— Simone Bertrand de Beauvoir, All Said and Done

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Sartre_and_de_Beauvoir_at_Balzac_Memorial.jpg/250px-Sartre_and_de_Beauvoir_at_Balzac_Memorial.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sartre_and_de_Beauvoir_at_Balzac_Memorial.jpg)

Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir at the Balzac Memorial

The family struggled to remain bourgeois after they lost much of their fortune shortly after [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") and Françoise's insistence his daughters attend a prestigious convent school.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-28) Because of her family's straitened circumstances she could no longer rely on her [dowry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dowry "Dowry"). This put her marriage opportunities at risk. She took this as an opportunity to work towards earning her own living.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-oxfordreference.com-29) She worked with [Maurice Merleau-Ponty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Merleau-Ponty "Maurice Merleau-Ponty") and [Claude Lévi-Strauss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_L%C3%A9vi-Strauss "Claude Lévi-Strauss"), when all three completed their practice teaching requirements at the same secondary school. From 1929 through 1943, Beauvoir taught at the [lycée](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyc%C3%A9e "Lycée") level until she could support herself solely on the earnings of her writings. She taught at the [Lycée Montgrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lyc%C3%A9e_Montgrand&action=edit&redlink=1 "Lycée Montgrand (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyc%C3%A9e_Montgrand "fr:Lycée Montgrand")) ([Marseille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marseille "Marseille")), the [Lycée Jeanne-d'Arc (Rouen)](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lyc%C3%A9e_Jeanne-d%27Arc_\(Rouen\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Lycée Jeanne-d'Arc (Rouen) (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyc%C3%A9e_Jeanne-d%27Arc_/(Rouen/) "fr:Lycée Jeanne-d'Arc (Rouen)")), and the [Lycée Molière (Paris)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyc%C3%A9e_Moli%C3%A8re_/(Paris/) "Lycée Molière (Paris)") (1936–39).[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-30)

During the trial of [Robert Brasillach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Brasillach "Robert Brasillach") in 1945 Beauvoir was among a small number of prominent intellectuals advocating for his execution for the 'intellectual crimes' of supporting [Fascism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fascism "Fascism") and the genocide of Jewish people. She defended this decision in her 1946 essay "An Eye for an Eye".[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-31)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-32)

Beauvoir and Jean-Paul Sartre met during her college years. Intrigued by her determination as an educator, he intended to make their relationship romantic. However, she had no interest in doing so.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-auto-25) She later changed her mind, and in October 1929, [Jean-Paul Sartre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Paul_Sartre "Jean-Paul Sartre") and Beauvoir became a couple for the next 51 years, until his death in 1980.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-33) After they were confronted by her father, Sartre asked her to marry him on a provisional basis. One day while they were sitting on a bench outside the Louvre, he said, "Let's sign a two-year lease".[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-34) Though Beauvoir wrote, "Marriage was impossible. I had no dowry", scholars point out that her ideal relationships described in _The Second Sex_ and elsewhere bore little resemblance to the marriage standards of the day.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-35)

> I think marriage is a very alienating institution, for men as well as for women. I think it's a very dangerous institution—dangerous for men, who find themselves trapped, saddled with a wife and children to support; dangerous for women, who aren't financially independent and end up by depending on men who can throw them out when they are 40; and very dangerous for children, because their parents vent all their frustrations and mutual hatred on them. The very words 'conjugal rights' are dreadful. Any institution which solders one person to another, obliging people to sleep together who no longer want to is a bad one.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-36)

Instead, she and Sartre entered into a lifelong "soul partnership", which was sexual but not exclusive, nor did it involve living together.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-37) She chose never to marry and never had children. This gave her the time to advance her education and engage in political causes, write and teach, and take lovers.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Schneir-38) Beauvoir's prominent open relationships at times overshadowed her academic reputation. A scholar who was lecturing with her[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-39) chastised their "distinguished \[Harvard\] audience \[because\] every question asked about Sartre concerned his work, while all those asked about Beauvoir concerned her personal life."[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-40)

Sartre and Beauvoir always read each other's work. Debate continues about the extent to which they influenced each other in their existentialist works, such as Sartre's _[Being and Nothingness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Being_and_Nothingness "Being and Nothingness")_ and Beauvoir's _She Came to Stay_ and "Phenomenology and Intent".[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-41) However, recent studies of Beauvoir's work focus on influences other than Sartre, including [Hegel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G._W._F._Hegel "G. W. F. Hegel") and Leibniz.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-SEP-Bergoffen-2010-8) The [Neo-Hegelian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Hegelianism "Neo-Hegelianism") revival led by [Alexandre Kojève](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Koj%C3%A8ve "Alexandre Kojève") and [Jean Hyppolite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Hyppolite "Jean Hyppolite") in the 1930s inspired a whole generation of French thinkers, including Sartre, to discover Hegel's _[Phenomenology of Spirit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phenomenology_of_Spirit "Phenomenology of Spirit")_.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-42)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-43) However, Beauvoir, reading Hegel in German during the war, produced an original critique of his dialectic of consciousness.

#### Allegations of sexual abuse

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Simone_de_Beauvoir&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Allegations of sexual abuse")\]

Beauvoir was [bisexual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bisexuality "Bisexuality"), and her relationships with young women were controversial.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Lise1-44) French author [Bianca Lamblin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bianca_Lamblin "Bianca Lamblin") (originally Bianca Bienenfeld) wrote in her book _Mémoires d'une jeune fille dérangée_ (Memoirs of a deranged young girl, published in English under the title _A Disgraceful Affair_) that, while a student at Lycée Molière, she was sexually exploited by her teacher Beauvoir, who was in her 30s.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-45) Beauvoir [groomed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_grooming "Sexual grooming") the 16-year-old girl before introducing her to Sartre. The three had a sexually exploitative relationship over the course of three years.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-:1-46) Bianca wrote her _Mémoires_ in response to the posthumous 1990 publication of Jean-Paul Sartre's _Lettres au Castor et à quelques autres: 1926-1963_ (Letters to Castor and other friends), in which she noted that she was referred to by the pseudonym Louise Védrine.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-47) Bianca, upon learning that she was given a pseudonym, stated she felt "nauseated and disgusted when \[she\] discovered the true personality of the woman \[she\] had loved all \[her\] life".[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-:1-46)

In 1943, Beauvoir was suspended again from her teaching position when she was accused of seducing her 17-year-old lycée pupil [Natalie Sorokine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natalie_Sorokin "Natalie Sorokin") in 1939.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-48) Sorokine's parents laid formal charges against Beauvoir for debauching a minor (the age of consent in France at the time was 13 until 1945, when it became 15)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-49)[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-50) and Beauvoir's licence to teach in France was revoked, although it was subsequently reinstated.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-51)

Beauvoir described in _La Force de l'âge_ (_The Prime of Life_) a relationship of simple friendship with Sorokine[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-52) (in the book referred to as "Lise Oblanoff").[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-53) However, both Sorokine and Lamblin—along with [Olga Kosakiewicz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olga_Kosakiewicz "Olga Kosakiewicz")—stated later that their relationships with Beauvoir had damaged them psychologically.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Lise1-44)

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/N%C3%BA%C3%B1ez-Beauvoir-Sartre-Che_Guevara.jpg/250px-N%C3%BA%C3%B1ez-Beauvoir-Sartre-Che_Guevara.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:N%C3%BA%C3%B1ez-Beauvoir-Sartre-Che_Guevara.jpg)

[Antonio Núñez Jiménez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_N%C3%BA%C3%B1ez_Jim%C3%A9nez "Antonio Núñez Jiménez"), Beauvoir, [Sartre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sartre "Sartre") and [Che Guevara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Che_Guevara "Che Guevara") in Cuba, 1960.

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/President_Nasser-Sagan-Sartre.jpg/250px-President_Nasser-Sagan-Sartre.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:President_Nasser-Sagan-Sartre.jpg)

[Egypt's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt "Egypt") President [Gamal Abdel Nasser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamal_Abdel_Nasser "Gamal Abdel Nasser"), Beauvoir, [Sartre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sartre "Sartre") and [Claude Lanzmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Lanzmann "Claude Lanzmann") in Cairo, 1967.

Beauvoir wrote popular travel diaries about time spent in the United States[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-54) and China and published essays and fiction rigorously, especially throughout the 1950s and 1960s. Her 1955 travels in China were the basis of her 1957 travelogue _[The Long March](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Long_March:_An_Account_of_Modern_China&action=edit&redlink=1 "The Long March: An Account of Modern China (page does not exist)")_, in which she praised the efforts of the Chinese communists to [emancipate women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feminism_in_Chinese_communism "Feminism in Chinese communism").[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Crean-55)

She published several volumes of short stories, including _The Woman Destroyed_, which, like some of her other later work, deals with aging. She lived with [Claude Lanzmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Lanzmann "Claude Lanzmann") from 1952 to 1959,[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-56) but perhaps her most famous lover was American author [Nelson Algren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Algren "Nelson Algren"). Beauvoir met Algren in Chicago in 1947, while she was on a four-month "exploration" trip of the United States using various means of transport: automobile, train, and [Greyhound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greyhound_Lines "Greyhound Lines"). She kept a detailed diary of the trip, which was published in France in 1948 with the title _America Day by Day_.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-57) She wrote to him across the Atlantic as "my beloved husband."[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-58) Algren won the National Book Award for _[The Man with the Golden Arm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Man_with_the_Golden_Arm_/(novel/) "The Man with the Golden Arm (novel)")_ in 1950, and in 1954, Beauvoir won France's [most prestigious literary prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prix_Goncourt "Prix Goncourt") for _[The Mandarins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mandarins "The Mandarins"),_ in which Algren is the character Lewis Brogan. Algren vociferously objected to their intimacy becoming public. Years after they separated, she was buried wearing his gift of a silver ring.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-59)

[![Image 7: Waist high portrait of middle aged man reading](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Nelson_Algren_NYWTS.jpg/250px-Nelson_Algren_NYWTS.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nelson_Algren_NYWTS.jpg)

Algren in 1956

When Beauvoir visited Algren in Chicago, [Art Shay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Shay "Art Shay") took well-known nude and portrait photos of Beauvoir. Shay also wrote a play based on Algren, Beauvoir, and Sartre's triangular relationship. The play was stage read in 1999 in Chicago.

Beauvoir also wrote a four-volume autobiography, consisting of _Memoirs of a Dutiful Daughter_, _The Prime of Life_, _Force of Circumstance_ (sometimes published in two volumes in English translation: _After the War_ and _Hard Times_), and _All Said and Done_.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-iep.utm.edu-60) In 1964 Beauvoir published a novella-length autobiography, _A Very Easy Death_, covering the time she spent visiting her aging mother, who was dying of cancer. The novella brings up questions of ethical concerns with truth-telling in doctor-patient relationships.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-61)

In the 1970s Beauvoir became active in France's [women's liberation movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women%27s_liberation_movement "Women's liberation movement"). She wrote and signed the [Manifesto of the 343](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifesto_of_the_343 "Manifesto of the 343") in 1971, a manifesto that included a list of famous women who claimed to have had an abortion, then illegal in France. Signatories were diverse\[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] as [Catherine Deneuve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Deneuve "Catherine Deneuve"), [Delphine Seyrig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphine_Seyrig "Delphine Seyrig"), and Beauvoir's sister Hélène. In 1974, abortion was legalized in France.

When asked in a 1975 interview with [Betty Friedan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Friedan "Betty Friedan") if she would support a minimum wage for women who do housework, Beauvoir answered: "No, we don’t believe that any woman should have this choice. No woman should be authorized to stay at home and raise her children. Society should be different. Women should not have that choice, precisely because if there is such a choice, too many women will make that one. It is a way of forcing women in a certain direction", further stating that motherhood "should be a choice, and not a result of conditioning”.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-62)[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-63)

In about 1976, Beauvoir and [Sylvie Le Bon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvie_Le_Bon-de_Beauvoir "Sylvie Le Bon-de Beauvoir") made a trip to New York City in the United States to visit [Kate Millett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kate_Millett "Kate Millett") on her farm.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-64)\[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\]

In 1977, Beauvoir signed a [petition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_petition_against_age_of_consent_laws "French petition against age of consent laws") along with other French intellectuals that supported the freeing of three arrested [paedophiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paedophile "Paedophile").[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Krizman-65)[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Henley-66) The petition explicitly addresses the 'Affaire de Versailles', where three adult men, Dejager (age 45), Gallien (age 43), and Burckhardt (age 39) had sexual relations with minors of both sexes aged 12–13.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-67)[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-68)

_[When Things of the Spirit Come First](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/When_Things_of_the_Spirit_Come_First "When Things of the Spirit Come First")_, a set of short stories Beauvoir had written decades previously but had not considered worth publishing, was released in 1980.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-iep.utm.edu-60)

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Sartre%2BBeauvoir_grave.JPG/250px-Sartre%2BBeauvoir_grave.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sartre%2BBeauvoir_grave.JPG)

Beauvoir's and Sartre's grave at the [Cimetière du Montparnasse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cimeti%C3%A8re_du_Montparnasse "Cimetière du Montparnasse").

In 1981 she wrote _La Cérémonie des adieux_ (_A Farewell to Sartre_), a painful account of Sartre's last years. In the opening of _Adieux_, Beauvoir notes that it is the only major published work of hers which Sartre did not read before its publication.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]

She contributed the piece "Feminism - Alive, Well, and in Constant Danger" to the 1984 anthology _[Sisterhood Is Global: The International Women's Movement Anthology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisterhood_Is_Global:_The_International_Women%27s_Movement_Anthology "Sisterhood Is Global: The International Women's Movement Anthology")_, edited by [Robin Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Morgan "Robin Morgan").[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-global-69)

After Sartre died in 1980, Beauvoir published his letters to her with edits to spare the feelings of people in their circle who were still living. After Beauvoir's death, Sartre's adopted daughter and literary heir [Arlette Elkaïm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlette_Elka%C3%AFm-Sartre "Arlette Elkaïm-Sartre") would not let many of Sartre's letters be published in unedited form. Most of Sartre's letters available today have Beauvoir's edits, which include a few omissions but mostly the use of pseudonyms. Beauvoir's adopted daughter and literary heir [Sylvie Le Bon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvie_Le_Bon-de_Beauvoir "Sylvie Le Bon-de Beauvoir"), unlike Elkaïm, published Beauvoir's unedited letters to both Sartre and Algren.

#### Sylvie Le Bon-de Beauvoir

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Simone_de_Beauvoir&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Sylvie Le Bon-de Beauvoir")\]

[Sylvie Le Bon-de Beauvoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvie_Le_Bon-de_Beauvoir "Sylvie Le Bon-de Beauvoir") and Simone de Beauvoir met in the 1960s, when Beauvoir was in her fifties and Sylvie was a teenager. In 1980, Beauvoir, 72, legally adopted Sylvie, who was in her late thirties, by which point they had already been in an intimate relationship for decades. Although Beauvoir rejected the institution of marriage her entire life, this adoption was like a marriage for her. Some scholars argue that this adoption was not to secure a literary heir for Beauvoir, but as a form of resistance to the bio-heteronormative family unit.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-70)

Beauvoir died of [pneumonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumonia "Pneumonia") on 14 April 1986 in Paris, aged 78.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-71) She is buried next to Sartre at the [Montparnasse Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montparnasse_Cemetery "Montparnasse Cemetery") in Paris.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-72) She was honored as a figure at the forefront of the struggle for women's rights around the time of her death.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Bergoffen-73)

[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Le_deuxi%C3%A8me_sexe.jpg/250px-Le_deuxi%C3%A8me_sexe.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Le_deuxi%C3%A8me_sexe.jpg)

_[The Second Sex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Second_Sex "The Second Sex")_

_[The Second Sex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Second_Sex "The Second Sex")_, first published in 1949 in French as _Le Deuxième Sexe_, turns the existentialist mantra that _[existence precedes essence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existence_precedes_essence "Existence precedes essence")_ into a feminist one: "One is not born but becomes a woman" (French: "On ne naît pas femme, on le devient").[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-74) With this famous phrase, Beauvoir first articulated what has come to be known as the [sex-gender distinction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex-gender_distinction "Sex-gender distinction"), that is, the distinction between biological sex and the social and historical construction of gender and its attendant stereotypes.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-75) Beauvoir argues that "the fundamental source of women's oppression is its \[femininity's\] historical and social construction as the quintessential" Other.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-76)

Beauvoir defines women as the "second sex" because women are defined as inferior to men. She pointed out that [Aristotle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle") argued women are "female by virtue of a certain lack of qualities", while [Thomas Aquinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Aquinas "Thomas Aquinas") referred to women as "imperfect men" and the "incidental" being.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-marxists.org-77) She quotes "In itself, homosexuality is as limiting as heterosexuality: the ideal should be to be capable of loving a woman or a man; either, a human being, without feeling fear, restraint, or obligation."[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-78)

Beauvoir asserted that women are as capable of choice as men, and thus can choose to elevate themselves, moving beyond the "[immanence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immanence "Immanence")" to which they were previously resigned and reaching "[transcendence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transcendence_/(philosophy/) "Transcendence (philosophy)")", a position in which one takes responsibility for oneself and the world, where one chooses one's freedom.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-79)

Chapters of _The Second Sex_ were originally published in _Les Temps modernes_,[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-80) in June 1949. The second volume came a few months after the first in France.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-81) It was published soon after in America due to the quick translation by [Howard Parshley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Parshley "Howard Parshley"), as prompted by [Blanche Knopf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanche_Knopf "Blanche Knopf"), wife of publisher [Alfred A. Knopf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_A._Knopf_Sr. "Alfred A. Knopf Sr."). Because Parshley had only a basic familiarity with the French language, and a minimal understanding of philosophy (he was a professor of biology at [Smith College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith_College "Smith College")), much of Beauvoir's book was mistranslated or inappropriately cut, distorting her intended message.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Moi,_Toril_2002-82) For years, Knopf prevented the introduction of a more accurate retranslation of Beauvoir's work, declining all proposals despite the efforts of existentialist scholars.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Moi,_Toril_2002-82)

Only in 2009 was there a second translation, to mark the 60th anniversary of the original publication. Constance Borde and Sheila Malovany-Chevallier produced the first integral translation in 2010, reinstating a third of the original work.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-83)

In the chapter "Woman: Myth and Reality" of _The Second Sex_,[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-84) Beauvoir argued that men had made women the "Other" in society by the application of a false aura of "mystery" around them. She argued that men used this as an excuse not to understand women or their problems and not to help them, and that this stereotyping was always done in societies by the group higher in the hierarchy to the group lower in the hierarchy. She wrote that a similar kind of oppression by hierarchy also happened in other categories of identity, such as race, class, and religion, but she claimed that it was nowhere more true than with gender in which men stereotyped women and used it as an excuse to organize society into a [patriarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriarchy "Patriarchy").\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]

Despite her contributions to the feminist movement, especially the French women's liberation movement, and her beliefs in women's economic independence and equal education, Beauvoir was initially reluctant to call herself a feminist.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-oxfordreference.com-29) However, after observing the resurgence of the feminist movement in the late 1960s and early 1970s, Beauvoir stated she no longer believed a [socialist revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutionary_socialism "Revolutionary socialism") to be enough to bring about women's liberation. She publicly declared herself a feminist in 1972 in an interview with _[Le Nouvel Observateur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Nouvel_Observateur "Le Nouvel Observateur")_.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-85)

In 2018, the manuscript pages of _Le Deuxième Sexe_ were published.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-86)

Other notable works
-------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Simone_de_Beauvoir&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Other notable works")\]

Beauvoir published her first novel _She Came to Stay_ in 1943.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-87) It has been assumed that it is inspired by her and Sartre's sexual relationship with [Olga Kosakiewicz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olga_Kosakiewicz "Olga Kosakiewicz") and [Wanda Kosakiewicz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wanda_Kosakiewicz "Wanda Kosakiewicz"). Olga was one of her students in the Rouen secondary school where Beauvoir taught during the early 1930s. She grew fond of Olga. Sartre tried to pursue Olga but she rejected him, so he began a relationship with her sister Wanda. Upon his death, Sartre was still supporting Wanda. He also supported Olga for years, until she met and married [Jacques-Laurent Bost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques-Laurent_Bost "Jacques-Laurent Bost"), a lover of Beauvoir. However, the main thrust of the novel is philosophical, a scene in which to situate Beauvoir's abiding philosophical pre-occupation – the relationship between the self and the other.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]

In the novel, set just before the outbreak of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Beauvoir creates one character from the complex relationships of Olga and Wanda. The fictionalised versions of Beauvoir and Sartre have a [ménage à trois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A9nage_%C3%A0_trois "Ménage à trois") with the young woman. The novel also delves into Beauvoir and Sartre's complex relationship and how it was affected by the ménage à trois.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]

_She Came to Stay_ was followed by many others, including _[The Blood of Others](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blood_of_Others "The Blood of Others")_, which explores the nature of individual responsibility, telling a love story between two young French students participating in the [Resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Resistance "French Resistance") in World War II.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-iep.utm.edu-60)

### Existentialist ethics

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Simone_de_Beauvoir&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Existentialist ethics")\]

[![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Simone_de_Beauvoir_%26_Jean-Paul_Sartre_in_Beijing_1955.jpg/250px-Simone_de_Beauvoir_%26_Jean-Paul_Sartre_in_Beijing_1955.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Simone_de_Beauvoir_%26_Jean-Paul_Sartre_in_Beijing_1955.jpg)

Simone de Beauvoir and Jean-Paul Sartre in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), 1955

Beauvoir wrote her first philosophical essay on existentialist ethics titled _[Pyrrhus et Cinéas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrrhus_and_Cineas "Pyrrhus and Cineas")_ (1944). The characters Pyrrhus and Cineas have a [socratic dialogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socratic_dialogue "Socratic dialogue") to discuss questions such as 'What are the criteria of ethical action?' and 'Can violence ever be justified?'.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-SEP-Bergoffen-2010-8)

She continued her exploration of existentialism through her second essay _[The Ethics of Ambiguity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ethics_of_Ambiguity "The Ethics of Ambiguity")_ (1947).

> She identifies herself as an existentialist and identifies existentialism as the philosophy of our (her) times because it is the only philosophy that takes the question of evil seriously. It is the only philosophy prepared to counter [Dostoevsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dostoevsky "Dostoevsky")'s claim \[in The Brothers Karamazov\][\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-88) that without God everything is permissible.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-SEP-Bergoffen-2010-8)

— Debra Bergoffen, Simone de Beauvoir, The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Fall 2010 Edition)

> 'But what will become of men then?' I asked him, 'without God and immortal life? All things are lawful then, they can do what they like?'

> Only the authentically moral attitude understands that the freedom of the self requires the freedom of others. To act alone or without concern for others is not to be free. **As Beauvoir explains, “No project can be defined except by its interference with other projects.”**

[![Image 11: Les Temps Modernes first issue cover.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/Les_Temps_modernes_n%C2%B01_oct._1945.png/250px-Les_Temps_modernes_n%C2%B01_oct._1945.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Les_Temps_modernes_n%C2%B01_oct._1945.png)

Les Temps Modernes first issue cover.

Beauvoir, Sartre, and [Maurice Merleau-Ponty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Merleau-Ponty "Maurice Merleau-Ponty") co-founded _[Les Temps Modernes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Temps_Modernes "Les Temps Modernes")_, a political journal that featured varied ideologies such as communists, Catholics, Gaullists, and socialists.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-:2-89) Sartre wrote the purpose of _Les Temps Modernes_ in the Preface of the first issue published on the 1st of October in 1945.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-:2-89)[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-90)

> Every writer of bourgeois origin has known the temptation of irresponsibility. I personally hold Flaubert personally responsible for the repression that followed the Commune because he did not write a line to try to stop it. It was not his business, people will perhaps say. Was the Calas trial Voltaire’s business? Was Dreyfus’s condemnation Zola’s business? We at Les Temps Modernes do not want to miss a beat on the times we live in. Our intention is to influence the society we live in. Les Temps Modernes will take sides.

— Jean-Paul Sartre, Les Temps Modernes, Preface

Beauvoir used _Les Temps Modernes_ to promote her own work and explore her ideas on a small scale before fashioning essays and books. Beauvoir remained an editor until her death. However, [Sartre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sartre "Sartre") and [Merleau-Ponty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merleau-Ponty "Merleau-Ponty") had a longstanding feud, which led Merleau-Ponty to leave _Les Temps modernes_. Beauvoir sided with Sartre and ceased to associate with Merleau-Ponty. In Beauvoir's later years, she hosted the journal's editorial meetings in her flat and contributed more than Sartre, whom she often had to force\[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] to offer his opinions.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]

[![Image 12](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Algren_house_Miller.jpg/250px-Algren_house_Miller.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Algren_house_Miller.jpg)

Dunes cottage where Algren and Beauvoir summered in [Miller Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miller_Beach "Miller Beach"), Indiana

Published in 1954, _The Mandarins_ won France's highest literary prize, the _[Prix Goncourt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prix_Goncourt "Prix Goncourt")_.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-91) It is a [roman à clef](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_%C3%A0_clef "Roman à clef") set after the end of World War II and follows the personal lives of philosophers and friends among Sartre's and Beauvoir's intimate circle, including her relationship with American writer [Nelson Algren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Algren "Nelson Algren"), to whom the book is dedicated.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-lrb_rogin-92)

Algren was outraged by the frank way Beauvoir described their sexual experiences in both _The Mandarins_ and her autobiographies.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-lrb_rogin-92) Algren vented his outrage when reviewing American translations of Beauvoir's work. Much material bearing on this episode in Beauvoir's life, including her love letters to Algren, entered the public domain only after her death.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-93)

Beauvoir's early novel _Les Inséparables_, long suppressed, was published in French in 2020 and two different English translations in 2021, by Sandra Smith in the US and [Lauren Elkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauren_Elkin "Lauren Elkin") in the UK.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-94) Written in 1954, the book describes her first love, a classmate named Elisabeth Lacoin ("Zaza") who died before age 22 of [viral encephalitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viral_encephalitis "Viral encephalitis"), and had as a teenager a "passionate and tragic" relationship with Beauvoir. According to [Sylvie Le Bon-de Beauvoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvie_Le_Bon-de_Beauvoir "Sylvie Le Bon-de Beauvoir"), Beauvoir never forgave Madame Lacoin for what happened, believing that Elisabeth-Zaza was murdered by the oppressive socio-cultural environment in which she had been raised.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-95) Disapproved by Sartre, the novel was deemed "too intimate" to be published during Beauvoir's lifetime.

Beauvoir's _[The Second Sex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Second_Sex "The Second Sex")_ is considered a foundational work in the history of feminism. Beauvoir had denied being feminist multiple times but ultimately admitted that she was one after _The Second Sex_ became crucial in the world of feminism.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Bergoffen-73) The work has had a profound influence, opening the way for [second-wave feminism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second-wave_feminism "Second-wave feminism") in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_wave_feminism_in_the_United_States "Second wave feminism in the United States"), [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_wave_feminism_in_Canada "Second wave feminism in Canada"), [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_wave_feminism_in_Australia "Second wave feminism in Australia"), and around the world.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-SEP-Bergoffen-2010-8) Although Beauvoir has been quoted as saying "There is a certain unreasonable demand that I find a little stupid because it would enclose me, immobilize me completely in a sort of feminist concrete block," her works on feminism have paved the way for all future feminists.[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Simone_de_Beauvoir:_An_Interview-96) The founders of the second-wave read _The Second Sex_ in translation, including [Kate Millett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kate_Millett "Kate Millett"), [Shulamith Firestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shulamith_Firestone "Shulamith Firestone"), [Juliet Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juliet_Mitchell "Juliet Mitchell"), [Ann Oakley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Oakley "Ann Oakley") and [Germaine Greer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germaine_Greer "Germaine Greer"). All acknowledged their profound debt to Beauvoir, including visiting her in France, consulting with her at crucial moments, and dedicating works to her.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Fallaize-1998-97) [Betty Friedan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Friedan "Betty Friedan"), whose 1963 book _[The Feminine Mystique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Feminine_Mystique "The Feminine Mystique")_ is often regarded as the opening salvo of second-wave feminism in the United States, later said that reading _The Second Sex_ in the early 1950s[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Fallaize-1998-97) "led me to whatever original analysis of women's existence I have been able to contribute to the Women's movement and its unique politics. I looked to Simone de Beauvoir for a philosophical and intellectual authority."[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Friedan-1975-98)

At one point in the early 1970s, Beauvoir also aligned herself with the French League for Women's Rights as a means to campaign and fight against sexism in French society.[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Simone_de_Beauvoir:_An_Interview-96) Beauvoir's influence goes beyond just her impact on second-wave founders, and extends to numerous aspects of feminism, including literary criticism, history, philosophy, theology, criticism of scientific discourse, and [psychotherapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychotherapy "Psychotherapy").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-SEP-Bergoffen-2010-8) When Beauvoir first became involved with the feminism movement, one of her objectives was legalizing abortion.[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Simone_de_Beauvoir:_An_Interview-96) [Donna Haraway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donna_Haraway "Donna Haraway") wrote that, "despite important differences, all the modern feminist meanings of gender have roots in Simone de Beauvoir's claim that 'one is not born a woman \[one becomes one\].'"[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-SEP-Bergoffen-2010-8) This "most famous feminist sentence ever written"[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Mann-2017-99) is echoed in the title of [Monique Wittig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monique_Wittig "Monique Wittig")'s 1981 essay _One Is Not Born a Woman_.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Fallaize-1998-97)[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-FOOTNOTEButler1990112-100)[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-McCann-Kim-2003-101) [Judith Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Butler "Judith Butler") took the concept a step further, arguing that Beauvoir's choice of the verb _to become_ suggests that [gender is a process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gender_performativity "Gender performativity"), constantly being renewed in an ongoing interaction between the surrounding culture and individual choice.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Fallaize-1998-97)[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-Bell-1999-102)

In Paris, [Place Jean-Paul-Sartre-et-Simone-de-Beauvoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Place_Jean-Paul-Sartre-et-Simone-de-Beauvoir "Place Jean-Paul-Sartre-et-Simone-de-Beauvoir") is a square where Beauvoir's legacy lives on. It is one of the few squares in Paris to be officially named after a couple. The pair lived close to the square at 42 [rue Bonaparte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rue_Bonaparte "Rue Bonaparte").

In 2019, _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_/(magazine/) "Time (magazine)")_ created 89 new covers to celebrate women of the year starting from 1920; it chose Beauvoir for 1949.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir#cite_note-103)
